Prevention: If there has been a severe outbreak of
Diplodia cob rot, destroy crop residues by grazing or ploughing in crop remains to a depth of 20 cm
Crop rotation with non host crops like bean, cassava and potato help reduce inoculum load
Rotate maize with soybean, potatoes and cassava for 2 years after a severe outbreak
Proper plant spacing should be used to decrease plants stress during growing season
Avoid mechanical damage that may be caused by insects and birds because it helps entry of pathogen into the cob
Harvest early to avoid cob rot if lodging is a concern
Monitoring: Monitor twice a week from early silking stage to 2-3 weeks after silking
This disease affects both the stems and the cobs of maize and is favoured by wet weather during silking
The first symptoms usually seen are drying of the husks and very small black specks (fungal reproductive structures) on the husk, cob and kernels.
When the husk is removed a grey/white mould can be seen growing on the kernels usually starting from the base to the tip of the cob
Diseased cobs should not be put into storage as they will infect healthy cobs
On the stems brown lesions embedded with small black dots on lower nodes can be seen and the pith is discoloured and rotten
Direct Control: Harvest early to reduce losses due to lodging following crop maturity
Remove infected cobs as soon as possible to remove disease from the field - do not put into storage
